<!-- readme-only -->

PaleoACES compares climate-predicted and observed forest composition in Mount Rainier (MORA) and
North Cascades (NOCA) National Parks, using forest resurveys and four Holocene macrofossil records.
One CCA calibrated on the legacy survey plots provides the shared coordinate system.

This page is the supplementary appendix of the analysis, in the order of the analysis: the research
questions, the study area, the forest tree communities, the climate products, climate change, fire
dynamics, the climate–community space, and then the four questions in turn (lags, pace and direction
effects, associations with fire, species contributions). It shows every main and supplementary figure,
the tables reported in the manuscript and the modelling code, and keeps the text of the Supporting
Information: Appendix S1 (age–depth models), Appendix S2 (climate products and the bias correction of the
paleoclimate), Appendix S3 (fire histories) and Appendix S4 (the analysis with the one-step correction and on
the raw paleoclimate). Data
cleaning is summarized by its figure here. The
step-by-step detail sits in [`report/details/`](report/details), linked from each section.

```sh
Rscript R/run_all.R --offline   # run the whole analysis from the cached climate (add --age-models to refit Bacon)
Rscript R/build_report.R        # rebuild this page and report/ from the outputs
```

# Supporting Information

This appendix follows the order of the Methods of the main text: the forest tree communities, the climate
products, climate change and the climate periods, fire dynamics, the climate–community space, and then the
four research questions (Q1 to Q4). It holds the supplementary figures (Figs. S1 to S17), the supplementary
tables (Tables S1 to S25), and four appendices: Appendix S1 (age–depth models of the Holocene records),
Appendix S2 (climate products and the bias correction of the Holocene climate), Appendix S3 (reconstruction
of the fire histories), and Appendix S4 (the analysis with a partial correction and without correction of
the Holocene climate).

Terms and units are those of the main text. MORA is Mount Rainier National Park and NOCA is the North
Cascades National Park Service Complex. The climate–community space is the space of the canonical
correspondence analysis (CCA), and a CCA distance is a distance in this space. Climate change is given in
standard deviations of the legacy plots (SD). In the tables, Holocene-S and Holocene-C are the Holocene
stability periods and the Holocene climate-change periods, MSpT is spring temperature, and SP is summer
precipitation. A lake-period is one lake within one climate period, from its oldest (t1) to its youngest
(t2) sampled century, and a plot pair is the legacy survey (t1) and the resurvey (t2) of a forest plot. A
positive pace effect, direction effect, or species contribution to the lag means that the lag was
amplified, and a negative one that it shrank. Analyses were run in R, with the packages rbacon 3.5.2,
tapas 0.1.5, and CharAnalysis 2.0.3 for the age–depth models and the fire histories.

<!-- /appendix-only -->

<!-- readme-only -->

# Research questions

The analysis compares forest community reassembly under Holocene and Anthropocene climate change in
Mount Rainier (MORA) and North Cascades (NOCA), in one climate–community ordination for both eras
(Fig. 1). It asks four questions (manuscript draft, November 2026), each answered in its own
section below:

1. Are climate–community lags smaller under slower Holocene climate change than under rapid
   Anthropocene climate change? ([Climate–community lags](#climatecommunity-lags-q1))
2. When communities fail to track climate, is this because observed community turnover is slower
   than climate-predicted turnover, because communities reorganize in a different direction from
   that predicted by climate, or both? ([Pace and direction effects](#pace-and-direction-effects-q2))
3. Is fire associated with differences in the pace and direction of climate tracking?
   ([Associations with fire](#associations-with-fire-q3))
4. Which species contribute the most to the discrepancies between observed and climate-predicted
   community change? ([Species contributions](#species-contributions-q4))

# Study area

The study covers Mount Rainier National Park (MORA) and the North Cascades National Park Service
Complex (NOCA), Washington, USA. In each park, legacy vegetation plots were resurveyed decades later,
and small lakes hold Holocene records in their sediments. Fig. 2 shows the plot pairs that enter
the CCA, whether each burned between the two surveys, and the cored lakes by what each record
contributes. At MORA, the vegetation comes from Jay Bath, Log Wallow and Reflection Pond (Dunwiddie
1986) and the fire from the Sunrise Ridge lakes of Walsh et al. (2017). At NOCA, vegetation and fire
come from the same core at Panther Potholes (Prichard et al. 2009).

```{r fig-2-study-area}
sa_n = function(p, v) sa[[v]][sa$site == p]
```

# Forest tree communities

## Legacy surveys and resurveys

<!-- readme-only -->

Legacy surveys and resurveys of the same plots at Mount Rainier (MORA) and North Cascades
(NOCA) National Parks were matched, cleaned and harmonized to one tree taxonomy
(`R/pipeline/01_clean_mora_vegetation.R`, `R/pipeline/02_clean_noca_vegetation.R`).

<!-- /readme-only -->

```{r fig-s01-occurrence-by-stage}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/figS01_tree_occurrence_by_stage.pdf')
```

**Fig. S1. Occurrence of tree species as adult trees and as seedlings in the legacy surveys and the
resurveys.** Number of plots in which each species was recorded as an adult tree or as a seedling at
Mount Rainier (MORA) and North Cascades (NOCA), after taxonomic harmonization and exclusion of
understory taxa, but before the selection of species for the CCA. A species could be recorded in both
stages in the same plot. At MORA, seedlings were individuals of 10–140 cm height in both surveys. At
NOCA, however, the legacy surveys recorded individuals of 0–3 m height as regeneration and taller
individuals as adults, whereas the resurveys recorded seedlings of 10–140 cm and adults taller than
1.4 m. Differences between the two stages at NOCA should therefore be interpreted with caution,
because the size classes differed between the surveys.

```{r fig-s02-plot-selection}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/figS02_plot_and_sample_selection.pdf')
```

**Fig. S2. Selection of forest plots and macrofossil samples for the canonical correspondence
analysis (CCA).** Flowchart of the matching, cleaning, and selection of the plot pairs (legacy survey
and resurvey; upper panels) and of the Holocene macrofossil samples (lower panels) at Mount Rainier
(MORA, blue) and North Cascades (NOCA, orange). The plot pairs that remained were used both to fit the
CCA (with the legacy surveys) and to quantify community change in the Anthropocene, whereas the
Holocene samples were projected into the fitted climate–community space. Plots without any of the
retained tree species at one of the two surveys were excluded, because they have no observed position
in this space. Sample sizes and reasons for exclusion are given at each step.

**Legacy plot size at NOCA.** Both parks were resurveyed with 500-m² plots, whereas the legacy plots
at NOCA ranged from 25 to 400 m². A small legacy plot can miss species that the larger resurvey plot
then records, which would be counted as community turnover. We therefore compared species richness,
turnover rate, lag, and lag rate among the legacy plot sizes of the NOCA plot pairs used in the analysis
(Table S1). This comparison is descriptive.

```{r vegetation-noca-plot-area}
pa = read_output('report/noca_plot_area_responses.csv')
pci = function(m, lo, hi) ifelse(is.na(lo), sprintf('%.3f', m), sprintf('%.3f (%.3f to %.3f)', m, lo, hi))
pa |> transmute(`Legacy area (m²)` = legacy_area, Plots = plots,
    `Richness, legacy` = sprintf('%.2f', richness_legacy_mean), `Richness, resurvey` = sprintf('%.2f', richness_resurvey_mean),
    `Turnover rate` = pci(turnover_rate_mean, turnover_rate_low, turnover_rate_high),
    Lag = pci(lag_mean, lag_low, lag_high), `Lag rate` = pci(lag_rate_mean, lag_rate_low, lag_rate_high)) |>
  show_table('noca_plot_area_responses', caption = paste('**Table S1. Plot pairs at NOCA by legacy plot size.** Richness is',
    'the mean number of the 14 tree species of the analysis that were present in a plot. Turnover rate, lag, and lag rate',
    'are means with 95% confidence intervals (t-intervals, no model): the turnover rate and the lag rate in CCA distance',
    'per century, and the lag in CCA distance. The single 36-m² plot has no interval.'))
pa_row = function(a) pa[pa$legacy_area == a, ]
```

The smallest legacy plots did not hold fewer species than the larger ones
(`r sprintf('%.2f', pa_row('25')$richness_legacy_mean)` species per 25-m² plot against
`r sprintf('%.2f', pa_row('100')$richness_legacy_mean)` per 100-m² plot), and their turnover rate was not higher
(`r sprintf('%.2f', pa_row('25')$turnover_rate_mean)` against
`r sprintf('%.2f', pa_row('100')$turnover_rate_mean)` CCA distance per century). The confidence intervals of
the three most common plot sizes overlapped for all quantities. The Anthropocene results at NOCA therefore
do not depend on the small legacy plots.

## Holocene macrofossil records

The Holocene communities come from plant macrofossils in dated lake-sediment cores, three at MORA and
one at NOCA (Fig. 2 of the main text). We dated each sample with the age–depth model of its core
(Appendix S1).

### Appendix S1. Construction of the Holocene age–depth models

#### S1.1 Why an age–depth model was required

The macrofossils are measured at known depths in a sediment core, but depth itself does not
provide an age. Sediment does not necessarily accumulate at a constant rate: for example, 1 cm of
sediment can represent relatively few years during rapid accumulation and many more years during
slow accumulation. Chronological control is available only at selected depths, through
radiocarbon dates, dated volcanic deposits, ²¹⁰Pb dating, or other independently dated horizons.
We therefore required an age–depth model to estimate the calendar age of every depth between
these dated points and, importantly, to quantify uncertainty in those estimated ages.

We used the rbacon R package, which reconstructs sediment accumulation histories within a Bayesian
framework (Blaauw & Christen 2011). Rather than drawing a single line through the dated horizons,
Bacon estimates many age–depth histories that are compatible with the chronological evidence and
assumptions about sediment accumulation. The distribution of these histories represents the
posterior chronological uncertainty shown in Fig. S4.

#### S1.2 Chronological controls and radiocarbon calibration

For each core, we assembled chronological controls for which both sediment depth and age
information were available (Table S2). For MORA, these consisted of the core surfaces, seven
radiocarbon dates from Jay Bath and Log Wallow, dated volcanic tephra horizons, and a basal
radiocarbon age for Reflection Pond. Reflection Pond contained no radiocarbon dates of its own and
was therefore constrained by the core surface, tephra horizons, and this basal control. For
Panther Potholes, we reproduced the chronology archived in the Neotoma database using the core
surface, five ²¹⁰Pb ages, six Accelerator Mass Spectrometry (AMS) radiocarbon dates, and three
tephra horizons. We used the corrected control depths archived in Neotoma rather than the depths
reported in Prichard et al. (2009), which contain documented depth errors.

Radiocarbon ages are expressed in ¹⁴C years and cannot be treated directly as calendar ages
because atmospheric ¹⁴C concentrations have varied through time. We therefore supplied
radiocarbon ages and their laboratory errors as uncalibrated dates (cc = 1), which Bacon
calibrated against the IntCal20 Northern Hemisphere calibration curve (Reimer et al. 2020). This
converts each radiocarbon measurement into a probability distribution of plausible calendar ages.
Controls already expressed in calendar years, including the core surfaces and tephra ages, were
supplied directly (cc = 0) and were not calibrated.

The seven MORA radiocarbon ages and their laboratory errors were taken directly from Dunwiddie
(1986). For all other chronological controls, the source and interpretation of the assigned age
uncertainty are reported explicitly in Table S2. The Reflection Pond basal control is the mean
of the two basal radiocarbon ages of Jay Bath (QL-1704) and Log Wallow (QL-1728), 6015 ± 110 ¹⁴C yr
BP with the larger of the two laboratory errors, following P. Dunwiddie's advice that the three
basins share the same basal age (pers. comm.).

For Panther Potholes, the five ²¹⁰Pb ages were derived using a Constant Rate of Supply (CRS)
model. We retained the error values used in the archived Gavin chronology for the primary model;
however, these values correspond numerically to the ²¹⁰Pb activity uncertainties reported by
Prichard et al. (2009), rather than to independently estimated age uncertainties in years. We
therefore evaluated this uncertainty specification in a separate sensitivity analysis described
below.

```{r table-s1-1}
read_output('table_S1_1_chronological_controls.csv', col_types = readr::cols(.default = 'c')) |>
  show_table('chronological_controls',
    caption = paste('**Table S2. Chronological controls used in the four Bayesian age–depth models.**',
      'For cc = 1, the entered age is an uncalibrated ¹⁴C age calibrated with IntCal20. For cc = 0,',
      'the entered age is already in calibrated years before present (cal yr BP; present = A.D. 1950).'))
```

#### S1.3 Bayesian age–depth models

We fitted each core independently with Bacon using the settings summarized in Table S3. Bacon
divided each sediment core into 5-cm sections and estimated an accumulation time, in yr cm⁻¹, for
each section. Accumulation times were allowed to differ among sections but were correlated between
neighbouring sections through the model's memory parameter. The chronological controls in
Table S2 were then used to update these prior expectations and generate the posterior age–depth
chronology shown in Fig. S4.

The three MORA cores were modelled using the same accumulation and memory priors. Panther Potholes
instead retained the settings of the archived Bacon chronology in the Neotoma database so that our
model reproduced the published chronology while providing the complete posterior age–depth draws
required for subsequent analyses. All runs are seeded (seed 42).

```{r table-s1-2}
read_output('table_S1_2_rbacon_parameters.csv', col_types = readr::cols(.default = 'c')) |>
  show_table('rbacon_parameters',
    caption = '**Table S3. rbacon parameters used to construct the age–depth models.**')
```

The thick volcanic deposits required one additional treatment. The MSH-Y tephra was represented as
an instantaneous depositional interval in all three MORA cores, including the 58-cm interval at Log
Wallow containing both primary and redeposited Y tephra. At Panther Potholes, the MSH-P, MSH-Y,
and Mazama tephra intervals were treated in the same way. Bacon therefore removed these intervals
while estimating gradual sediment accumulation and reinserted them without adding elapsed time.
These intervals are shown as vertical grey bands in Fig. S4.

```{r fig-s04-age-depth}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/figS04_age_depth_models.pdf')
```

**Fig. S4. Bayesian age–depth models for the Jay Bath, Log Wallow, and Reflection Pond cores at
MORA and the Panther Potholes core at NOCA.** For each core, the three upper panels show, from left
to right, the Markov chain Monte Carlo trace, the prior (green) and posterior (grey) distributions
of sediment accumulation time, and the prior and posterior distributions of memory. In the main
panels, depth increases along the x-axis and age is expressed as calibrated years before present.
Coloured distributions at dated depths represent the chronological controls and their
uncertainty. The grey field represents the posterior distribution of possible age–depth
relationships; the central red line shows the posterior age–depth estimate and the outer dotted
lines the 95% posterior interval. Vertical grey bands identify tephra intervals treated as
instantaneous deposition.

For Panther Potholes, we reproduced the archived Neotoma chronology as the primary model. However,
Prichard et al. (2009) report uncertainties for measured ²¹⁰Pb activity, in DPM g⁻¹, and the same
numerical values were entered as age errors, in years, in the archived chronology. We therefore
fitted a sensitivity model in which the five ²¹⁰Pb controls were each assigned an assumed ±10-year
age error, all other controls and settings unchanged (Fig. S5).

```{r fig-s05-pb210}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/figS05_panther_potholes_pb210_sensitivity.pdf')
```

**Fig. S5. Sensitivity of the Panther Potholes age–depth chronology to uncertainty assigned to the
five ²¹⁰Pb controls in the upper 35 cm of the core.** The left panel shows that the two posterior
chronologies are nearly identical below the ²¹⁰Pb-dated section, whereas the right panel shows the
expected increase in uncertainty within the upper 35–40 cm. The uncertainty assigned to the ²¹⁰Pb
controls affects the precision of the most recent chronology but does not materially alter the
deeper Holocene chronology used in our analyses.

# Climate products

## Appendix S2. Climate products and the bias correction of the Holocene climate

```{r appendix-s2-setup}
s2_points = read_output('climate_products_points.csv')
s2_factors = read_output('climate_bias_correction_factors.csv')
s2_check = read_output('climate_trace_cruts_check.csv')
s2_n = function(k, p) sum(s2_points$kind == k & s2_points$site == p)
s2_rng = function(x, d = 1) sprintf(paste0('%.', d, 'f to %.', d, 'f'), min(x), max(x))
s2_fr = function(p, v) s2_factors |> filter(site == p, variable == v)
s2_ck = function(p, pl, v) s2_check |> filter(site == p, place == paste(p, pl), variable == v)
s2_dt = function(p, pl) { d = s2_ck(p, pl, 'MSpT')$difference; sprintf('%.2f °C %s', abs(d), if (d > 0) 'warmer' else 'cooler') }
```

We fitted the climate–community space with CHELSA V2.1 at the forest plots, whereas the climate-predicted
positions of the Holocene communities come from CHELSA-TraCE21k at the lakes. If the two products differ in
the level of temperature or precipitation, a Holocene climate is placed elsewhere in the climate–community
space than the same climate would be with CHELSA V2.1, and this difference enters every mismatch and every
lag. We therefore corrected the Holocene climate to the level of CHELSA V2.1.

Four CHELSA products cover the two parks (Table S4). CHELSA V2.1 is the most recent one and the product of
the Anthropocene analysis, so we kept it and corrected CHELSA-TraCE21k. The most recent time step of
CHELSA-TraCE21k is the mean of the years 1900 to 1990 (technical specification, Table 4), and not the present
climate. CHELSAcruts covers 1901 to 2016 and therefore has years in common with both CHELSA-TraCE21k and
CHELSA V2.1, so we used it as the link between them. Note that CHELSA-TraCE21k, CHELSAcruts, and CHELSA V1.2
are downscaled with the CHELSA V1 method, and CHELSA V2.1 with the more recent method.

**Table S4. The four CHELSA products.** All four products have the same grid of 30 arcsec.

| Product | Version | Years read | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| CHELSA-TraCE21k | 1.0 | timeIDs 16 to 20 (1500 to 1990, century means) | Downscaled TraCE-21k transient simulation; timeID 20 is the mean of 1900 to 1990 |
| CHELSAcruts | 1.0 | 1901 to 2016, monthly | CRU TS anomalies downscaled with the CHELSA V1 climatology |
| CHELSA V1.2 | 1.2.1 | 1979 to 2013, monthly | CHELSA time series, first version |
| CHELSA V2.1 | 2.1 | 1979 to 2021, monthly | CHELSA time series, current version; the climate of the climate–community space |

We read each product at all forest plots (`r s2_n('plot', 'MORA')` at MORA and `r s2_n('plot', 'NOCA')` at
NOCA), at the grid cells of the four lakes, and at all grid cells within 5 km of the lakes of each park
(`r s2_n('disc', 'MORA')` grid cells around the midpoint of the three MORA lakes, and `r s2_n('disc', 'NOCA')`
around Panther Potholes).<!-- readme-only --> Script: [`R/pipeline/07_climate_products.R`](R/pipeline/07_climate_products.R).<!-- /readme-only -->

### S2.1 CHELSA-TraCE21k against CHELSAcruts

CHELSA-TraCE21k and CHELSAcruts are downscaled with the same method, so they could be expected to agree
over the years that they have in common. They did not. Over 1900 to 1990, on the grid cells within 5 km of
the lakes, CHELSA-TraCE21k was `r s2_dt('MORA', 'disc')` in spring and had
`r sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * s2_ck('MORA', 'disc', 'SP')$ratio)` of the summer precipitation of CHELSAcruts at
MORA, and was `r s2_dt('NOCA', 'disc')` with `r sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * s2_ck('NOCA', 'disc', 'SP')$ratio)` of
the summer precipitation at NOCA (Table S5). At the forest plots, the same comparison gave
`r s2_dt('MORA', 'plots')` and `r sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * s2_ck('MORA', 'plots', 'SP')$ratio)` at MORA, and
`r s2_dt('NOCA', 'plots')` and `r sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * s2_ck('NOCA', 'plots', 'SP')$ratio)` at NOCA. At the grid
cells of the lakes, it gave `r s2_dt('MORA', 'lakes')` and
`r sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * s2_ck('MORA', 'lakes', 'SP')$ratio)` at MORA (mean of the three lakes), and
`r s2_dt('NOCA', 'lakes')` and `r sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * s2_ck('NOCA', 'lakes', 'SP')$ratio)` at Panther Potholes.
The differences were larger for the monthly variables: around the MORA lakes, CHELSA-TraCE21k was
`r s2_rng(-s2_fr('MORA', 'tasmin')$step1, 1)` °C warmer in minimum temperature, depending on the month
(Fig. S6). Because the two products did not agree around the lakes, we first corrected CHELSA-TraCE21k to
CHELSAcruts.

```{r appendix-s2-check}
s2_check |> filter(variable %in% c('MSpT', 'SP')) |>
  arrange(site, match(place, paste(rep(c('MORA', 'NOCA'), each = 3), c('disc', 'lakes', 'plots'))), variable) |>
  transmute(Park = site, Place = place, Variable = c(MSpT = 'Spring temperature (°C)', SP = 'Summer precipitation (mm)')[variable],
    `TraCE21k timeID 20` = trace, `CHELSAcruts 1901-1990` = cruts, Difference = difference, Ratio = ratio) |>
  show_table('appendix_s2_trace_cruts_check', digits = 2, caption = paste('**Table S5. CHELSA-TraCE21k against CHELSAcruts over',
    'the same years.** The most recent time step of CHELSA-TraCE21k (timeID 20, the mean of 1900 to 1990) and CHELSAcruts',
    '(1901 to 1990), on the grid cells within 5 km of the lakes (disc), at the grid cells of the lakes (MORA: mean of the',
    'three lakes), and as the mean over the forest plots. Difference: CHELSAcruts subtracted from CHELSA-TraCE21k.',
    'Ratio: CHELSA-TraCE21k divided by CHELSAcruts.'))
```

### S2.2 The two-step bias correction

We corrected the Holocene climate in two steps. We calculated both steps for each park, calendar month, and
variable (monthly minimum temperature, maximum temperature, and precipitation, and not the seasonal
variables), from the mean over the grid cells within 5 km of the lakes of the park, and not from the single
grid cells of the lakes. In step 1, we corrected CHELSA-TraCE21k to CHELSAcruts over the years 1900 to 1990
(CHELSAcruts starts in 1901). In step 2, we corrected CHELSAcruts to CHELSA V2.1 over all years that the
two products have in common (`r min(s2_factors$step2_first)` to `r max(s2_factors$step2_last)`). For
temperature, each step is an offset that we added, and for precipitation, a ratio by which we multiplied.
We applied both steps to all time steps of CHELSA-TraCE21k at all lakes of the park, and used this corrected
Holocene climate in the main analysis.<!-- readme-only --> Script: [`R/pipeline/08_paleo_climate.R`](R/pipeline/08_paleo_climate.R).<!-- /readme-only -->

Note that this correction assumes that the difference between the products was constant through the
Holocene. We therefore repeated the analysis with step 2 alone (one-step correction, which assumes that
CHELSA-TraCE21k and CHELSAcruts agree) and without correction (Appendix S4).

```{r fig-s08-correction}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/figS06_climate_bias_correction.pdf')
```

**Fig. S6. The two steps of the bias correction of the Holocene climate.** For each park and calendar month,
the offset added to temperature (°C) or the ratio by which precipitation was multiplied, calculated on the
grid cells within 5 km of the lakes. Purple: step 1 (CHELSA-TraCE21k to CHELSAcruts, 1900 to 1990). Grey:
step 2 (CHELSAcruts to CHELSA V2.1, 1979 to 2016), with the 10th to 90th percentile of the yearly values in
light grey. Red: both steps together, i.e., the correction of the main analysis. On the dashed line, a step
changes nothing.<!-- readme-only --> Script: [`R/figures/supp_climate_products.R`](R/figures/supp_climate_products.R).<!-- /readme-only -->

Across the months, the two steps together changed the minimum temperature at MORA by
`r s2_rng(s2_fr('MORA', 'tasmin')$two_step, 1)` °C and the maximum temperature by
`r s2_rng(s2_fr('MORA', 'tasmax')$two_step, 1)` °C, and multiplied precipitation by
`r s2_rng(s2_fr('MORA', 'pr')$two_step, 2)`. At NOCA, they changed the minimum temperature by
`r s2_rng(s2_fr('NOCA', 'tasmin')$two_step, 1)` °C and the maximum temperature by
`r s2_rng(s2_fr('NOCA', 'tasmax')$two_step, 1)` °C, and multiplied precipitation by
`r s2_rng(s2_fr('NOCA', 'pr')$two_step, 2)` (Fig. S6). Step 2 alone would have changed the two temperatures at
MORA by `r s2_rng(s2_fr('MORA', 'tasmin')$step2, 1)` °C and `r s2_rng(s2_fr('MORA', 'tasmax')$step2, 1)` °C, and
multiplied precipitation by `r s2_rng(s2_fr('MORA', 'pr')$step2, 2)`. How the correction affected the results is
shown in Appendix S4.<!-- readme-only --> The stage writes the factors of every park, variable and month to
`climate_bias_correction_factors.csv`. `r details_link('02_climate', 'Climate details')`.<!-- /readme-only -->

# Climate change and comparisons within eras

## Climate data

<!-- readme-only -->

Modern climate is CHELSA V2.1 monthly climate in a survey-specific window for every plot
(`R/pipeline/04_modern_climate.R`); Holocene climate is CHELSA-TraCE21k at each lake and century,
bias-corrected onto CHELSA V2.1 (Appendix S2; `R/pipeline/08_paleo_climate.R`).

<!-- /readme-only -->

climate from CHELSA V2.1 (1979–2021), averaged over the plot pairs at Mount Rainier (MORA, blue) and
North Cascades (NOCA, orange), for mean annual temperature (MAT), annual precipitation (AP), and the four
seasonal variables, i.e., mean spring temperature (MSpT), mean winter temperature (MWT), summer
precipitation (SP), and winter precipitation (WP). Spring temperature and summer precipitation are the
two variables of the climate–community space. The shaded area shows the climate window of the legacy

## Climate periods

<!-- readme-only -->

**What and why.** The Holocene is cut into climate-change (C) periods, when the park-average
climate of the lakes moved steadily in one direction, and stability (S) periods between them. The
rules of the climate-era step are unchanged. Only their input changed: the periods are now drawn
from the two CCA variables, MSpT and SP, so that the periods describe change along the same
climate axes that the CCA uses. A climate-change period that contains a long internal trough of
low change is split into sub-periods (a, b, c). Each period, or sub-period, is one unit for the
lake-periods (see Climate–community lags).

**Result.**

<!-- /readme-only -->

```{r step1-periods}
comparison = read_output('holocene_period_comparison.csv')
comparison |> transmute(Catalog = catalog, Period = period, Type = period_type,
    `Older (cal BP)` = older_cal_bp, `Younger (cal BP)` = younger_cal_bp,
    `Duration (years)` = duration_years, Drivers = gsub(';', ', ', coalesce(drivers, ''))) |>
  show_table('step1_periods', caption = paste('**Table S6. Climate periods of the Holocene.** Climate-change (C) and',
    'stability (S) periods defined from spring temperature (MSpT) and summer precipitation (SP), which are used in the',
    'analysis, and, with the same rules, from the four seasonal variables, for comparison. Drivers: the variables whose',
    'change defined a climate-change period.'))
periods = comparison |> filter(startsWith(catalog, 'MSpT'))
# Boundaries of the four-variable periods quoted in the text below.
four_bound = function(id, col) comparison[[col]][startsWith(comparison$catalog, 'All') & comparison$period == id]
```

<!-- readme-only -->

With MSpT and SP the Holocene from `r max(periods$older_cal_bp)` to `r min(periods$younger_cal_bp)`
cal BP falls into `r sum(periods$period_type == 'Holocene-C')` climate-change periods and
`r sum(periods$period_type == 'Holocene-S')` stability periods, and no climate-change period is
split. The first four-variable climate-change period (C1a to C1c, `r four_bound('C1a', 'older_cal_bp')` to
`r four_bound('C1c', 'younger_cal_bp')` cal BP) becomes C1, S1 and C2: its middle part
(`r four_bound('C1b', 'older_cal_bp')` to `r four_bound('C1b', 'younger_cal_bp')` cal BP) was driven by winter
wetting alone, which is no longer a constraint. From `r four_bound('C1c', 'younger_cal_bp')` cal BP onward every
boundary is unchanged, and the periods are
renumbered.

<!-- /readme-only -->

<!-- readme-only -->

```{r fig-3-main}
show_figure('report/figures/main/fig_climate_levels_eras_fire.pdf')
rates2 = read_output('figures/anthropocene_climate_rates.csv')
r2 = function(v, park) { x = rates2[rates2$variable == v & rates2$site == park, ]
  if (v == 'SP') sprintf('%+.0f mm (%+.1f SD)', x$rate, x$z_rate) else sprintf('%+.2f °C (%+.1f SD)', x$rate, x$z_rate) }
```

**Fig. 3. Holocene climate and fire.** (A) Spring temperature (°C) and (B) summer
precipitation (mm), the two CCA constraints, averaged over the lakes of each park with the two parks
weighted equally (CHELSA-TraCE21k). Bold lines are 1,000-year running means and thin lines the
centennial series. Shading marks the climate-change (C) and stability (S) periods, with the change
that drove each climate-change period written below its name (cooling or warming of spring temperature, drying or
wetting of summer precipitation). Labels linked to the bold lines give the change per century over a period for each
variable that drove it. A cross marks the largest step between two consecutive centuries, labelled with its rate. To the right of each panel, the Anthropocene change per century from
the legacy to the resurvey climate window, the median over plots in each park: spring temperature
`r sprintf('%+.2f', rates2$rate[rates2$variable == 'MSpT' & rates2$site == 'MORA'])` °C at MORA and
`r sprintf('%+.2f', rates2$rate[rates2$variable == 'MSpT' & rates2$site == 'NOCA'])` °C at NOCA, summer precipitation
`r sprintf('%+.1f', rates2$rate[rates2$variable == 'SP' & rates2$site == 'MORA'])` mm at MORA and
`r sprintf('%+.1f', rates2$rate[rates2$variable == 'SP' & rates2$site == 'NOCA'])` mm at NOCA. These come from a change
over about 29 years, while each Holocene rate spans a whole period of 400 to 2,700 years. (C) Fire
frequency of each park: accepted fire events per 1,000 years, counted in a 1,000-year window centred
every 100 years. At MORA it is the mean of the three Sunrise Ridge cores of Walsh et al. (2017) wherever
at least two cover the date, at NOCA the Panther Potholes core (Prichard et al. 2009). The two parks are
on different y axes because their frequencies are not comparable: Panther Potholes is resampled every 12
years and the Sunrise Ridge cores every 42 to 48 years, and a finer record resolves more events. The
MORA cores lie on Sunrise Ridge, away from the vegetation lakes (Fig. S12). The models do not use this
curve: their fire activity counts the same accepted events between the two ends of each lake-period,
per century and per covered core (see Climate–community lags). To the right, the Anthropocene plot pairs of each park that
burned between the two surveys (MORA's two burned plots are left out of the analysis).

# Fire dynamics

## Appendix S3. Reconstruction of fire histories

### S3.1 Holocene charcoal records

For MORA, we reconstructed Holocene fire activity using the Sunrise Lake, Shadow Lake, and Little
Sunrise Lake macrocharcoal records from Walsh et al. (2017). These records provide evidence of
regional fire activity on Sunrise Ridge and are independent of the Jay Bath, Log Wallow, and
Reflection Pond records that we used for the forest communities. For NOCA, we reconstructed Holocene fire
activity using the Panther Potholes macrocharcoal record of Prichard et al. (2009), extracted from
the archived Neotoma record and dated with the Panther Potholes chronology of Appendix S1. Thus,
at NOCA, the fire record and the forest record come from the same core and have the same chronology.

### S3.2 Identification of individual fire events

We reconstructed the fire-event detection analyses of Walsh et al. (2017) and Prichard et al.
(2009) within one workflow, with the R package tapas<!-- readme-only -->
(`R/pipeline/09_fire_records.R`)<!-- /readme-only -->. The charcoal accumulation rate (CHAR) was interpolated to regular intervals, its slowly varying
background estimated by robust LOWESS, and candidate fire events identified where the residual
peak component exceeded a record-specific threshold of the background noise. Candidates were
screened with a 75-year minimum-count test (p ≤ 0.05), and consecutive exceedances were treated as
one event. Record-specific settings are given in Table S7.

```{r table-s2-1}
events = read_output('holocene_fire_source_events.csv') |> count(lake, name = 'Accepted fire events')
read_output('holocene_fire_source_settings.csv') |>
  left_join(events, by = 'lake') |>
  transmute(Site = site, `Fire record` = if_else(lake == 'PantherPotholes', 'Panther Potholes', lake),
    `Interpolation interval (years)` = interpolation_years,
    `Background window (years)` = smoothing_years,
    `Peak threshold` = paste0(100 * threshold_probability, '%'), `Accepted fire events`) |>
  show_table('fire_detection_parameters',
    caption = paste('**Table S7. Parameters used to reconstruct individual Holocene fire events.**',
      'All records were also screened with the same 75-year minimum-count test (p ≤ 0.05).',
      'MORA settings follow Walsh et al. (2017) and Panther Potholes settings Prichard et al. (2009),',
      'except its 12-year interpolation interval, the median resolution of our updated chronology.'))
```

```{r fig-s10-fire-events}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/figS11_fire_event_detection.pdf')
```

**Fig. S11. Identification of Holocene fire events in the four records.** The residual peak
component is the difference between interpolated charcoal accumulation rates (CHAR) and the
background estimated with the record's robust LOWESS window. Candidate events exceed the local
noise threshold (dashed line) and are then screened with a 75-year minimum-count test
(p ≤ 0.05): filled circles are accepted events, and red crosses are rejected candidates.

### S3.3 Fire frequency

We counted the accepted events of each record within centred 1,000-year windows evaluated every 100
years and expressed them as events per 1,000 years. The MORA series is the mean of the three Sunrise
Ridge records wherever at least two of them cover the date, and the NOCA series is the Panther Potholes
record<!-- readme-only --> (`R/pipeline/12_climate_eras_fire_frequency.R`)<!-- /readme-only -->. Fig. 3C of the main text shows both
series, each park with its own axis, because the records differ in resolution and their fire frequencies
therefore cannot be compared between the parks. Note that the models do not use this fire frequency: they
use the number of fire events between t1 and t2 of each lake-period (see Methods of the main text).<!-- readme-only --> No
high-fire periods are classified: an earlier version marked periods above the park's median plus one
robust standard deviation, but no model used them, and the frequency itself is shown instead.<!-- /readme-only -->

### S3.4 Reproducibility against the original studies

We compared the number of events identified by tapas with those reported by Walsh et al. (2017)
and Prichard et al. (2009), and additionally reproduced the MORA analyses with CharAnalysis R
2.0.3 (Table S8). Event counts differed from the published values, including with CharAnalysis,
suggesting that discrepancies arise partly from differences between software implementations. We
retained tapas for one consistent detection procedure across all four records, preserving their
source-specific settings rather than tuning parameters to reproduce published counts.

```{r table-s2-2}
# Published Panther Potholes total: Prichard et al. (2009), as in the Supporting Information draft.
PRICHARD_2009_PUBLISHED_EVENTS = 59L
mora = read_output('walsh_charanalysis_software_comparison.csv') |>
  transmute(Site = 'MORA', Lake = sub(' Lake$', '', lake), Published = published_total_episodes,
    `CharAnalysis R 2.0.3` = official_r_episodes, tapas = tapas_episodes)
noca = tibble(Site = 'NOCA', Lake = 'Panther Potholes', Published = PRICHARD_2009_PUBLISHED_EVENTS,
  `CharAnalysis R 2.0.3` = NA_real_, tapas = events$`Accepted fire events`[events$lake == 'PantherPotholes'])
difference = function(t, p) sprintf('%+d (%+.0f%%)', as.integer(t - p), 100 * (t - p) / p)
rows = bind_rows(
  mora |> arrange(match(Lake, c('Sunrise', 'Shadow', 'Little Sunrise'))),
  mora |> summarise(Site = 'MORA total', Lake = '', across(c(Published, `CharAnalysis R 2.0.3`, tapas), sum)),
  noca,
  bind_rows(mora, noca) |> summarise(Site = 'Both sites', Lake = '', Published = sum(Published),
    `CharAnalysis R 2.0.3` = NA_real_, tapas = sum(tapas))) |>
  mutate(`Difference from published` = difference(tapas, Published))
show_table(rows, 'fire_event_counts', digits = 0,
  caption = paste('**Table S8. Holocene fire-event counts reported in the original studies and',
    'reconstructed with CharAnalysis R 2.0.3 (MORA only) and tapas (all four records).**'))
```

## Charcoal of the fire records and of the forest records at MORA

```{r fig-s11-charcoal}
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/figS12_charcoal_walsh_dunwiddie.pdf')
cc = read_output('figures/charcoal_dunwiddie_walsh_correlations.csv')
cm = read_output('figures/charcoal_dunwiddie_walsh_event_matching.csv')
cr = function(rec, what) { x = cc[cc$record == rec & cc$against == what, ]; sprintf('%+.2f (p = %.2f)', x$rho, x$p_shift) }
acc = 'Walsh charcoal accumulation (mean of three cores)'; frq = 'Walsh fire frequency (mean of three cores)'
bench = cc[cc$against == 'Walsh core against core', ]
```

**Fig. S12. Charcoal in the fire records of Sunrise Ridge (Walsh et al., 2017) and in the forest records
of MORA (Dunwiddie, 1986).** The fire activity of MORA comes from the three Sunrise Ridge records, whereas
the forest communities come from Jay Bath, Log Wallow, and Reflection Pond. The upper three rows show the
charcoal accumulation rate of each Sunrise Ridge record (grey), with its background (dashed) and the fire
events that we identified (dark red triangles). The lower three rows show the number of charcoal fragments
in each macrofossil sample of Dunwiddie (1986). This number is a concentration, because all samples of a
core had the same volume, and the samples above the 75th percentile of each lake are filled. Each fire
event of the Sunrise Ridge records is drawn as a faint line through all rows. Time runs from 7,000 cal BP
to the present, which is the time span of the forest records. The two kinds of record followed opposite
long-term courses: the Sunrise Ridge records hold most of their charcoal and fire events in the last 3,500
years, whereas Jay Bath and Log Wallow hold most of their charcoal before 4,000 cal BP. We correlated the
charcoal of each forest record with the mean of the three Sunrise Ridge records over `r unique(cc$bins)[1]`
bins of 500 years (Spearman correlation, with p from circular shifts that keep the autocorrelation of each
record, so that the smallest possible p is about 0.07). Jay Bath gave `r cr('Jay Bath', acc)` with the
charcoal accumulation rate and `r cr('Jay Bath', frq)` with the fire frequency, Log Wallow
`r cr('Log Wallow', acc)` and `r cr('Log Wallow', frq)`, and Reflection Pond `r cr('Reflection Pond', acc)`
and `r cr('Reflection Pond', frq)`. The Sunrise Ridge records agreed only weakly with one another
(`r paste(sprintf('%s %+.2f', bench$record, bench$rho), collapse = ', ')`). A charcoal peak of the forest
records lay within 200 years of `r sprintf('%.0f', 100 * cm$matched[cm$record == 'Jay Bath'])`%,
`r sprintf('%.0f', 100 * cm$matched[cm$record == 'Log Wallow'])`%, and
`r sprintf('%.0f', 100 * cm$matched[cm$record == 'Reflection Pond'])`% of the `r cm$walsh_events[1]` fire events
of Sunrise Ridge at Jay Bath, Log Wallow, and Reflection Pond, against
`r sprintf('%.0f', 100 * cm$chance[cm$record == 'Jay Bath'])`%,
`r sprintf('%.0f', 100 * cm$chance[cm$record == 'Log Wallow'])`%, and
`r sprintf('%.0f', 100 * cm$chance[cm$record == 'Reflection Pond'])`% expected by chance. The Sunrise Ridge
records therefore give no evidence of the fire history at the lakes of the forest records, and the fire
activity of MORA should be interpreted as regional at best. Note that the charcoal of the forest records
is a concentration and not an accumulation rate, so that a change in sedimentation rate could explain part
of its long-term course.<!-- readme-only --> Script:
[`R/figures/supp_charcoal_dunwiddie_walsh.R`](R/figures/supp_charcoal_dunwiddie_walsh.R).<!-- /readme-only -->

<!-- readme-only -->

## Fire between the two surveys

In the Anthropocene a plot pair counts as burned when a fire falls between its two surveys. At MORA
this comes from the National Park Service LandTrendr landscape-change polygons of 1987 to 2017 (a
fire polygon within 100 m of the plot), at NOCA from the assignment of Wilson et al. (2024). Of the
plot pairs in the analysis, `r sa_n('MORA', 'burned')` at MORA and `r sa_n('NOCA', 'burned')` at NOCA
burned (Figs. 2 and 3C). The two MORA plots that burned are left out of the analysis, so the
Anthropocene fire comparison is a NOCA comparison.

<!-- /readme-only -->

# Climate–community space

<!-- readme-only -->

One CCA is fitted to the legacy composition of the `r cca_value('calibration_plots')` matched
plots (MORA and NOCA pooled), constrained by the climate variables above (scaling 1, Hill = FALSE).
Resurvey plots and Holocene samples are projected into it: their climate gives a predicted (LC)
position and their composition an observed (WA) position.

**What and why.** The four seasonal variables come in two tightly linked pairs: spring and winter
temperature, and summer and winter precipitation. Inside a pair the CCA cannot tell the two
seasons apart, and Holocene lakes reach seasonal combinations the modern plots never show. The CCA
is therefore constrained by one variable of each pair. Spring temperature (MSpT) stands for
snowmelt timing and the start of the growing season. Summer precipitation (SP) stands for summer
drying stress. Because each pair is strongly correlated, the two also carry temperature and
precipitation change in general.

**How it is calculated.**

```{r step0-code}
code_snippet('R/pipeline/11_cca.R', 'cca-fit')
code_snippet('R/pipeline/11_cca.R', 'cca-projection')
```

**Result.**

<!-- /readme-only -->

```{r step0-screening}
screening = read_output('cca_screening.csv')
screening |> group_by(set) |> summarise(Variables = gsub(';', ', ', first(variables)),
    `Largest abs. correlation` = first(max_abs_correlation),
    `VIF` = paste(sprintf('%s %.1f', variable, VIF), collapse = ', '),
    `R²` = first(R2), `Adjusted R²` = first(adjusted_R2),
    `MORA lake-centuries outside (%)` = 100 * first(extrapolated_share_MORA),
    `NOCA lake-centuries outside (%)` = 100 * first(extrapolated_share_NOCA), .groups = 'drop') |>
  arrange(match(set, c('All four', 'MWT + SP', 'MSpT + SP'))) |> rename(Set = set) |>
  show_table('step0_screening', caption = sprintf(paste('**Table S9. Choice of the climate variables of the climate–community space.**',
    'CCA fitted to the %d legacy plots with three sets of climate variables. VIF, variance inflation factor. The last two columns',
    'give the percentage of the centuries of the Holocene records (%d at MORA, three lakes, and %d at NOCA) whose climate was',
    'outside the climate of the legacy plots.'),
    screening$n_plots[1], screening$holocene_lake_centuries_MORA[1], screening$holocene_lake_centuries_NOCA[1]))
addback = read_output('cca_screening_addback.csv')
rotation = read_output('cca_display_rotation.csv')
```

<!-- readme-only -->

With MSpT and SP the CCA explains `r sprintf('%.1f%%', 100 * screening$adjusted_R2[screening$set == 'MSpT + SP'][1])`
of the variation in composition (adjusted R²), against
`r sprintf('%.1f%%', 100 * screening$adjusted_R2[screening$set == 'All four'][1])` with all four
variables. Adding winter temperature and winter precipitation back improves the fit
(pseudo-F `r sprintf('%.2f', addback$pseudo_F[1])`, p = `r sprintf('%.4f', addback$p_value[addback$design == 'Unrestricted'])`
unrestricted and p = `r sprintf('%.4f', addback$p_value[addback$design == 'Within parks'])` within parks).
That gain comes from the seasonal contrasts within each pair, the same contrasts that make the
four-variable fit collinear (VIF up to `r sprintf('%.1f', max(screening$VIF[screening$set == 'All four']))`)
and that place `r sprintf('%.0f%%', 100 * screening$extrapolated_share_MORA[screening$set == 'All four'][1])`
of the MORA lake-centuries outside the calibration climate. With MSpT and SP no lake-century in
either park is outside it. The display rotation turns the plane by
`r sprintf('%.1f', rotation$angle_degrees)` degrees so that rotated axis 1 is spring temperature
increasing to the right and rotated axis 2 summer precipitation increasing upward. The pipeline
asserts that mismatch, lag, turnover, pace and direction are identical before and after this rotation.

**Choice of CCA constraints.** Candidate variables are screened by their correlations (Fig. S8)
and by their variance inflation in the fitted CCA, keeping one temperature and one precipitation
variable. With the four seasonal variables MSpT, MWT, SP and WP, the two temperatures had variance
inflation factors near 30 and opposite-signed coefficients that are not identifiable. The CCA is
therefore constrained by spring temperature, the temperature that changes most through the
Holocene, and summer precipitation. Figures in the CCA plane are rotated rigidly by the varimax
angle so that the two arrows lie along the axes; distances and angles, and therefore every
tracking metric, are unchanged by the rotation (decision of 2026-11-09 in
`r details_link('10_decisions', 'Decisions')`). The constraints of this build:

<!-- /readme-only -->

```{r cca-vif}
read_output('cca_climate_contributions.csv') |>
  transmute(Variable = variable, Label = variable_label, VIF, `CCA1 score` = CCA1, `CCA2 score` = CCA2) |>
  show_table('cca_constraint_vif', digits = 2, caption = paste('**Table S10. The two climate variables of the climate–community space.**',
    'Variance inflation factor (VIF) and biplot score of each variable on the two unrotated CCA axes.'))
```

```{r cca-axes}
read_output('cca_axes.csv') |>
  transmute(Axis = axis, Eigenvalue = eigenvalue, `% total inertia` = percent_total_inertia,
    `% constrained inertia` = percent_constrained_inertia) |>
  show_table('cca_axes', caption = sprintf('**Table S11. Axes of the CCA.** The two climate variables explained %.1f%% of the variation in composition (constrained inertia).',
    as.numeric(cca_value('constrained_percent'))))
read_output('cca_anova.csv') |>
  transmute(Test = test, Component = component, df, `Pseudo-F` = pseudo_F,
    `p (unrestricted)` = p_unrestricted, `p (within parks)` = p_within_parks) |>
  show_table('cca_permutation_tests', caption = paste('**Table S12. Permutation tests of the CCA.** 9,999 permutations,',
    'unrestricted and restricted within parks. df, degrees of freedom of each component.'))
```

## Holocene samples in the climate–community space

<!-- readme-only -->

**What and why.** Each macrofossil sample has an observed position in the CCA plane (its WA score,
from the taxa it contains). Each lake also has a climate-predicted position for every century
(its LC score, from that lake's own climate cell). Samples are dated by the median of their Bacon
ages and grouped by century. The observed position of a century is the centroid of its samples'
WA positions. No vegetation is interpolated between sampled centuries. These century positions
feed the lake-periods (Climate–community lags) and the period centroids of Fig. 4. No model is fitted on the
century steps any more.

<!-- /readme-only -->

```{r step1-positions}
positions = read_output('cca_tracking_holocene_century_positions.csv')
positions |> group_by(Park = site, Lake = lake) |>
  summarise(`Sampled centuries` = n(), Samples = sum(n_samples),
    `Centuries with one sample` = sum(n_samples == 1),
    `Oldest (cal BP)` = max(century_cal_bp), `Youngest (cal BP)` = min(century_cal_bp), .groups = 'drop') |>
  show_table('step1_sampled_centuries', caption = '**Table S13. Sampled centuries of each lake.** A sampled century is a century with at least one macrofossil sample.')
```

The records of the three MORA lakes start at about `r format(max(positions$century_cal_bp[positions$site == 'MORA']), big.mark = ',')`
cal BP, and most of their sampled centuries hold a single sample. The Panther Potholes record (NOCA) covers
the whole Holocene, with several samples per century.

[`R/helpers/century_tracking.R`](R/helpers/century_tracking.R),
[`R/helpers/tracking_metrics.R`](R/helpers/tracking_metrics.R).

# Climate–community lags (Q1)

## Lake-periods

<!-- readme-only -->

**What and why.** Two scoops of sediment from the same forest in the same century differ by
about as much as the forest drifts in many centuries, because one needle caught or missed moves a
sample's position. A lag computed between consecutive centuries is therefore mostly that noise.
Comparing the two ends of a whole climate period lets the drift outgrow it. A lake-period is one
lake within one climate period. Its start (t1) is the oldest and its end (t2) the youngest
sampled century of that lake in that period, and a lake needs samples in at least two centuries
of a period to have a lake-period there. The centuries in between enter no model.

At each end the mismatch M is the distance between the observed and the climate-predicted
positions. The lag rate is the change in M per century. The turnover rate is the length of the
observed movement per century. The pace and direction effects ask how much smaller the final
mismatch would have been if the community had moved the predicted distance in its own direction
(pace) or its own distance in the predicted direction (direction). The climate change rate is the
standardized end-to-end change of MSpT and SP in the lake's own climate cell, per century. Fire
activity is the number of accepted fire events between t1 and t2, per century and per charcoal
core, averaged over the cores of the park that cover the whole lake-period.

**How it is calculated.** The code below computes every quantity from the two ends of a unit, a
Holocene lake-period or an Anthropocene plot pair. The comments say what each step means.

```{r step24-code}
code_snippet('R/helpers/tracking_metrics.R', 'tracking-geometry')
code_snippet('R/helpers/tracking_metrics.R', 'tracking-corrections')
```

**Result.**

<!-- /readme-only -->

```{r step24-units}
candidates = read_output('cca_tracking_lake_period_candidates.csv')
units = read_output('cca_tracking_lake_periods.csv')
units |> transmute(Park = site, Lake = lake, Period = period, `t1 (cal BP)` = age_start,
    `t2 (cal BP)` = age_end, `Years` = duration_yr, `Samples t1` = n_start, `Samples t2` = n_end,
    `Climate change rate` = climate_rate, `MSpT change (°C)` = MSpT_change, `SP change (mm)` = SP_change,
    `Fire activity` = fire_activity, `M t1` = M_start, `M t2` = M_end, `Lag rate` = lag_rate,
    `Turnover rate` = turnover_rate, `Pace effect` = pace_effect, `Direction effect` = direction_effect) |>
  show_table('step24_lake_periods', caption = paste('**Table S14. Lake-periods.** One row for each lake within each climate',
    'period, from its oldest (t1) to its youngest (t2) sampled century. M, climate–community mismatch. Rates are per century:',
    'the climate change rate in SD of the legacy plots, fire activity in fire events per charcoal record, and the other rates',
    'in CCA distance. The pace effect and the direction effect are undefined when the observed or the climate-predicted',
    'position did not move.'))
```

Of the `r nrow(candidates)` combinations of lake and climate period with at least one sampled century,
`r nrow(units)` had samples in two or more centuries and are therefore lake-periods
(`r sum(units$site == 'MORA')` at MORA and `r sum(units$site == 'NOCA')` at NOCA, of which
`r sum(units$period_type == 'Holocene-C')` in climate-change periods and
`r sum(units$period_type == 'Holocene-S')` in stability periods). The lake-periods span
`r min(units$duration_yr)` to `r max(units$duration_yr)` years. At MORA, t1 and t2 of every lake-period hold
a single sample, and `r sum(!units$direction_defined & units$site == 'MORA')` lake-periods have no pace or
direction effect, because the observed or the climate-predicted position did not move. The charcoal
records cover all lake-periods.

## Comparison among period types

<!-- readme-only -->

**What and why.** Each response is compared between the Holocene stability periods, the
Holocene climate-change periods and the Anthropocene, within each park. The two Holocene types
are never pooled, so back-and-forth change in the stability periods cannot cancel the directional
change of the climate-change periods, and the parks are never pooled. The Holocene rows are the
lake-periods and the Anthropocene rows are the plot pairs, in one model per response with
group-specific residual spread, the endpoint weights and the AR(1) within each lake. Fire stays
out of these models, because it is measured differently in the two eras. Rates over a few decades
and over centuries are not on equal footing, since longer windows give lower rates, and every
comparison states both time spans. The three contrasts between period types in each park are tested
together for both parks, so each response has six contrasts, and their p-values are Holm-adjusted
within that family. Significance is read from the adjusted p-values. The intervals are the unadjusted
95% intervals.

**How it is calculated.**

```{r q1-code}
code_snippet('R/pipeline/14_era_models.R', 'era-model')
```

**Result.**

<!-- /readme-only -->

```{r step5a-results}
era_dir = 'era_comparison'
means = read_output(file.path(era_dir, 'era_means.csv'))
contrasts = read_output(file.path(era_dir, 'era_contrasts.csv'))
folds = read_output(file.path(era_dir, 'era_folds.csv'))
durations = read_output(file.path(era_dir, 'era_durations.csv'))
response_label = c(climate_rate = 'Climate change rate', climate_change = 'Climate change (not divided by time)',
  pace_effect_total = 'Pace effect (not divided by time)', direction_effect_total = 'Direction effect (not divided by time)',
  turnover_rate = 'Turnover rate',
  displacement = 'Turnover (not divided by time)', lag_rate = 'Lag rate', lag = 'Lag',
  pace_effect = 'Pace effect', direction_effect = 'Direction effect')
span = function(type) { d = durations[durations$period_type == type, ]; sprintf('%g to %g', min(d$duration_min), max(d$duration_max)) }
spans = sprintf(paste('The lake-periods span %s years in the Holocene climate-change periods and %s years in the',
  'Holocene stability periods, and the Anthropocene plot pairs span %s years.'), span('Holocene-C'), span('Holocene-S'), span('Anthropocene'))
means |> transmute(Quantity = response_label[response], Park = site, `Period type` = period_type, n,
    `Estimated mean` = estimate, SE = std_error, df, `95% CI` = sprintf('%.3f to %.3f', conf_low, conf_high)) |>
  show_table('step5a_era_means', caption = paste('**Table S15. Comparison among period types: estimated means for each period type and park.**',
    'Generalized least-squares models with period type, park, and their interaction as fixed effects (see Methods of the main text).',
    'SE, standard error. df, residual degrees of freedom of the model, used for the 95% confidence interval (CI). Climate change',
    'is in SD of the legacy plots, and turnover, lag, pace effect, and direction effect are in CCA distance. The quantities named',
    '"rate", and the pace effect and the direction effect without "(not divided by time)", are per century.', spans))
contrasts |> transmute(Quantity = response_label[response], Park = site, Contrast = contrast,
    Estimate = estimate, SE = std_error, df, t = estimate / std_error,
    `95% CI` = sprintf('%.3f to %.3f', conf_low, conf_high), p = p_value, `p (Holm)` = p_adjusted) |>
  show_table('step5a_era_contrasts', caption = paste('**Table S16. Comparison among period types: differences between period types within',
    'each park.** Models and units as in Table S15. Two-sided t-tests on the residual degrees of freedom (df) of the model, with 95%',
    'confidence intervals (CI, not adjusted). p (Holm) is adjusted with the Holm method across the six differences of each quantity,',
    'three per park.', spans))
folds |> transmute(Quantity = response_label[response], Park = site, `Anthropocene over` = against,
    Fold = fold, `Quoted as speed` = ifelse(quoted_as_speed, 'yes', 'no')) |>
  show_table('step5a_era_folds', caption = paste('**Table S17. How many times higher the rates were in the Anthropocene than in the Holocene.**',
    'The estimated mean of the Anthropocene divided by the estimated mean of each Holocene period type (Table S15).', spans))
fold = function(r, p, a) folds$fold[folds$response == r & folds$site == p & folds$against == a]
holm_p = function(p) ifelse(p < .001, 'Holm p < 0.001', sprintf('Holm p = %.3f', p))
ct = function(r, p, k) { x = contrasts[contrasts$response == r & contrasts$site == p & contrasts$contrast == k, ]
  sprintf('%+.2f (%.2f to %.2f, %s)', x$estimate, x$conf_low, x$conf_high, holm_p(x$p_adjusted)) }
```

<!-- readme-only -->

Climate changed `r sprintf('%.0f', fold('climate_rate', 'MORA', 'Holocene-C'))` times faster at MORA
and `r sprintf('%.0f', fold('climate_rate', 'NOCA', 'Holocene-C'))` times faster at NOCA in the
Anthropocene than in the Holocene climate-change periods. The forest turned over
`r sprintf('%.0f', fold('turnover_rate', 'MORA', 'Holocene-C'))` times faster at MORA and
`r sprintf('%.0f', fold('turnover_rate', 'NOCA', 'Holocene-C'))` times faster at NOCA. At MORA the lag
grew in the Anthropocene and did not grow in either Holocene type (Anthropocene minus Holocene-C
`r ct('lag_rate', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')`, minus Holocene-S
`r ct('lag_rate', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-S')` CCA distance per century). At NOCA the lag
rate did not differ between the period types (`r ct('lag_rate', 'NOCA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')`
against Holocene-C). `r cs = contrasts |> filter(contrast == 'Holocene-C - Holocene-S', response %in% c('lag', 'lag_rate', 'pace_effect', 'pace_effect_total', 'direction_effect', 'direction_effect_total'), p_adjusted < .05); if (nrow(cs)) paste0('Within the Holocene, the C and S lake-periods differed in ', paste(sprintf('the %s at %s (%s)', tolower(response_label[cs$response]), cs$site, mapply(ct, cs$response, cs$site, cs$contrast)), collapse = ' and '), ', and in no other lag, pace or direction response.') else 'Within the Holocene, the C and S lake-periods did not differ in lag, pace or direction in either park.'` `r spans`

Not divided by time, the climate still shifted further in the few decades of the Anthropocene than
over a whole Holocene lake-period (Anthropocene minus Holocene-C
`r ct('climate_change', 'MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')` calibration SD at MORA,
`r ct('climate_change', 'NOCA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C')` at NOCA). The distance the community moved
(the displacement) tells a different story
from its rate: in a few decades the plots moved about as far as, or further than, the Holocene communities
did over whole lake-periods. Anthropocene minus Holocene, in CCA distance:
`r moved = function(p, k) { x = contrasts[contrasts$response == 'displacement' & contrasts$site == p & contrasts$contrast == k, ]
  sprintf('%s %s the %s periods (%s)', p, if (x$p_adjusted < .05) ifelse(x$estimate > 0, 'moved further than in', 'moved less far than in')
    else 'did not differ significantly from', ifelse(grepl('-C$', k), 'climate-change', 'stability'), ct('displacement', p, k)) }
  paste(c(moved('MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C'), moved('MORA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-S'),
    moved('NOCA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-C'), moved('NOCA', 'Anthropocene - Holocene-S')), collapse = '; ')`.

<!-- /readme-only -->

<!-- readme-only -->

```{r fig-5-main}
show_figure('report/figures/main/fig_era_contrasts.pdf')
```

**Fig. 5. Climate change, community turnover and climate-community lag in the Holocene and the Anthropocene.**
For each park, the fitted mean and 95% confidence interval of the Holocene stability periods (triangles), the
Holocene climate-change periods (circles) and the Anthropocene plot pairs (diamonds). Each row shows a total between
the two ends of a lake-period or plot pair (left) and its rate per century (right): (A) the standardized climate
change, the distance between the climates at the two ends, and (B) its rate; (C) the observed community turnover,
the distance the community moved in CCA space, and (D) its rate; (E) the climate-community lag, the change in
mismatch between the two ends (M at t2 minus M at t1), and (F) its rate. The fitted mean is printed beside each
point. B and D are on log axes, where equal distances are equal folds, and the arrow gives the fold between the
Anthropocene and the Holocene climate-change means. A, C, E and F are on linear axes without folds. Their connectors
link the Anthropocene to the Holocene climate-change periods (lower) and to the Holocene stability periods (upper)
within each park, and a star marks a contrast that differs from zero (two-sided t test, Holm-adjusted p < 0.05
across the six period-type contrasts of each response, three per park). The intervals are unadjusted. The totals in A,
C and E build up over a whole lake-period in the Holocene and over the few decades between the two surveys in the
Anthropocene. Means come from the model response ~ period type × site, with an
AR(1) correlation within each lake and weights for the number of samples at each end, fitted on
`r n_group('Holocene-C', 'MORA')` climate-change and `r n_group('Holocene-S', 'MORA')` stability lake-periods and
`r n_group('Anthropocene', 'MORA')` plot pairs at MORA, and `r n_group('Holocene-C', 'NOCA')`, `r n_group('Holocene-S', 'NOCA')`
and `r n_group('Anthropocene', 'NOCA')` at NOCA. `r both_spans` Longer windows give lower rates, so the rates of the
two eras are not on equal footing. Units: the climate change rate in calibration standard deviations per century,
the climate change in calibration standard deviations, the turnover and lag rates in CCA distance per century,
the turnover and the lag in CCA distance.

<!-- /readme-only -->

**Turnover and lag by the duration of the lake-periods.** Turnover and lag are not divided by time, so a
longer lake-period could have more of both only because it is longer. Table S18 gives their means (no
model) for three classes of duration.

```{r step5a-duration-classes}
dc = read_output(file.path(era_dir, 'era_duration_classes.csv'))
dc |> transmute(Park = site, Duration = duration_class, `Lake-periods` = lake_periods,
    `Stability / climate-change` = sprintf('%d / %d', stability, climate_change),
    Years = sprintf('%g to %g', duration_min, duration_max), `Mean turnover` = mean_displacement,
    `Mean absolute lag` = mean_absolute_lag, `Mean lag` = mean_lag) |>
  show_table('step5a_duration_classes', caption = paste('**Table S18. Turnover and lag of the lake-periods by duration.**',
    'Means over the Holocene lake-periods of each park and class of duration. Turnover is the distance that the community',
    'moved in the climate–community space between t1 and t2. The absolute lag is the size of the change in mismatch between',
    't1 and t2 without its sign, and the lag is the same change with its sign. All three are in CCA distance and not divided',
    'by time.'))
dd = function(p, k, v) dc[[v]][dc$site == p & dc$duration_class == k]
```

At MORA, the `r dd('MORA', '1,000 years or more', 'lake_periods')` longest lake-periods
(`r format(dd('MORA', '1,000 years or more', 'duration_min'), big.mark = ',')` to `r format(dd('MORA', '1,000 years or more', 'duration_max'), big.mark = ',')` years)
had a higher turnover than the shorter ones
(mean of `r sprintf('%.3f', dd('MORA', '1,000 years or more', 'mean_displacement'))` against
`r sprintf('%.3f', dd('MORA', '200 to 400 years', 'mean_displacement'))` for 200 to 400 years and
`r sprintf('%.3f', dd('MORA', '500 to 900 years', 'mean_displacement'))` for 500 to 900 years). At NOCA,
turnover did not increase with duration (`r sprintf('%.3f', dd('NOCA', '200 to 400 years', 'mean_displacement'))`,
`r sprintf('%.3f', dd('NOCA', '500 to 900 years', 'mean_displacement'))`, and
`r sprintf('%.3f', dd('NOCA', '1,000 years or more', 'mean_displacement'))`, the last from a single
lake-period). The absolute lag ranged from `r sprintf('%.3f', min(dc$mean_absolute_lag[dc$site == 'MORA']))` to
`r sprintf('%.3f', max(dc$mean_absolute_lag[dc$site == 'MORA']))` at MORA and from
`r sprintf('%.3f', min(dc$mean_absolute_lag[dc$site == 'NOCA']))` to
`r sprintf('%.3f', max(dc$mean_absolute_lag[dc$site == 'NOCA']))` at NOCA among the classes. Turnover is the
net movement of the community between t1 and t2, so movements back and forth within a lake-period do not
add to it, and it does not increase in proportion to time. This is one reason why the rates of the long
lake-periods are low.

**Model checks.** Each model of the comparison among period types is a generalized least-squares model
with period type, park, and their interaction as fixed effects, a first-order autoregressive correlation
between successive lake-periods of a lake, and a residual standard deviation for each period type and park
(relative to the Anthropocene at MORA), multiplied by the square root of the variance that comes from the
number of samples at t1 and t2 (see Methods of the main text). Table S19 gives, for each model, the number
of lake-periods and plot pairs, the number of coefficients, the residual degrees of freedom, the residual
standard error, the parameters of the correlation and of the variances, the restricted log-likelihood, the
AIC, and a descriptive R². Fig. S14 shows the residuals.<!-- readme-only --> The coefficients of every model are on the
`r details_link('08_models', 'model details page')`.<!-- /readme-only -->

```{r q1-model-checks}
read_output('era_comparison/era_model_summary.csv') |>
  transmute(Quantity = response_label[response], Units = n, Coefficients = coefficients, `Residual df` = df_residual,
    `Residual SE` = sigma, `AR(1)` = AR1_phi,
    `Residual SD by period type and park` = gsub('A[.]', '', gsub(';', ', ', variance_parameters)),
    `Log-likelihood (REML)` = log_lik_REML, AIC, `Descriptive R²` = R2, Warnings = coalesce(warnings, 'none')) |>
  show_table('era_model_summary', caption = paste('**Table S19. Comparison among period types: fit of the models.**',
    'Units, number of lake-periods and plot pairs. AR(1), parameter of the first-order autoregressive correlation between',
    'successive lake-periods of a lake. The residual standard deviation (SD) of each period type and park is relative to that of',
    'the Anthropocene at MORA, and is multiplied by the square root of the variance from the number of samples at t1 and t2.',
    'Residual df, units with the coefficients subtracted. The residual SE is that of the Anthropocene at MORA for a variance',
    'of 1. The models were fitted with restricted maximum likelihood (REML), so that the log-likelihood and the AIC can only be',
    'compared among models with the same fixed effects. R² is descriptive (the residual sum of squares divided by the total',
    'sum of squares, subtracted from 1).'))
show_figure('report/figures/supplementary/figS14_era_model_residuals.pdf')
```

**Fig. S14. Residuals of the ten models of the comparison among period types.** Top: normal quantile
plots of the normalized residuals, one for each quantity. Bottom: normalized residuals for each period
type and park (points, with boxes for the quartiles). The models have no continuous explanatory variable,
so the fitted values take one value for each period type and park, and the residuals for each group show
what a plot against the fitted values would show. Climate change, climate change rate, turnover, and
turnover rate are positive by construction, and their residuals are skewed to the right. The residuals of
the lag, the lag rate, and the pace and direction effects have heavy tails, which come from a few
Anthropocene plot pairs.

# Pace and direction effects (Q2)

<!-- readme-only -->

**What and why.** The pace effect and the direction effect, defined with the lake-periods above, ask
whether a lag comes from how far the community moved or from the direction it took. They are compared
between the period types with the same era models as the lag (code, fit statistics and residuals in
Q1: Table S19, Fig. S14).

**Result.**

<!-- /readme-only -->

```{r step5-era-words}
# The era contrasts of a response in words, from their Holm-adjusted p, so that the text follows the fit.
era_words = function(r, p) {
  x = contrasts |> filter(response == r, site == p, contrast != 'Holocene-C - Holocene-S')
  k = sub('Anthropocene - ', '', x$contrast); v = mapply(ct, r, p, x$contrast)
  if (!any(x$p_adjusted < .05)) return(sprintf('does not differ from either Holocene type (%s against %s)', v[1], k[1]))
  paste(ifelse(x$p_adjusted < .05, sprintf('%s that of %s (%s)', ifelse(x$estimate > 0, 'exceeds', 'falls below'), k, v),
    sprintf('does not differ from %s (%s)', k, v)), collapse = ' and ')
}
totals = contrasts |> filter(response %in% c('pace_effect_total', 'direction_effect_total'),
  contrast != 'Holocene-C - Holocene-S')
totals_sig = totals |> filter(p_adjusted < .05)
```

<!-- readme-only -->

Per century, the MORA pace effect of the Anthropocene `r era_words('pace_effect', 'MORA')`, and the MORA direction
effect `r era_words('direction_effect', 'MORA')`. At NOCA the per-century pace effect
`r era_words('pace_effect', 'NOCA')`, and the direction effect `r era_words('direction_effect', 'NOCA')`. Not divided
by time, `r if (nrow(totals_sig)) paste0(nrow(totals_sig), ' of the ', nrow(totals), ' contrasts between the Anthropocene and a Holocene period type ', if (nrow(totals_sig) == 1) 'is' else 'are', ' significant after the adjustment: ', paste(sprintf('%s at %s, %s (%s)', tolower(response_label[totals_sig$response]), totals_sig$site, totals_sig$contrast, mapply(ct, totals_sig$response, totals_sig$site, totals_sig$contrast)), collapse = '; ')) else paste0('none of the ', nrow(totals), ' contrasts between the Anthropocene and a Holocene period type is significant after the adjustment')`.
The Anthropocene effects are large per century mainly because they build up over a few decades.

```{r fig-6-main}
show_figure('report/figures/main/fig_lag_pace_direction.pdf')
```

**Fig. 6. Pace effect and direction effect in the Holocene and the Anthropocene.** For each park, the fitted
mean and 95% confidence interval of the Holocene stability periods (triangles), the Holocene climate-change periods
(circles) and the Anthropocene (diamonds), with the fitted mean printed beside each point. Each row shows an effect
over the whole lake-period or plot pair (left, not divided by time) and per century (right): (A) the pace effect
and (B) the pace effect per century, (C) the direction effect and (D) the direction effect per century. All four
panels share one y scale. Each effect is the lag at the end of the period minus the lag the community would have had at the
climate-predicted pace (A, B, keeping its own direction) or in the climate-predicted direction (C, D, keeping its
own distance). A positive effect means that the community's own pace or direction widened the lag. A negative
effect means that it narrowed the lag. Connectors link the Anthropocene to the Holocene climate-change periods
(lower) and to the Holocene stability periods (upper) within each park, and a star marks a contrast that differs

panel F shows the lag rate. Lake-periods and plots whose observed or predicted position did not move have no pace or direction effect: the panels
hold `r m5 = read_output('era_comparison/era_means.csv'); m5$n[m5$response == 'pace_effect' & m5$site == 'MORA' & m5$period_type == 'Holocene-C']` climate-change and `r m5$n[m5$response == 'pace_effect' & m5$site == 'MORA' & m5$period_type == 'Holocene-S']` stability lake-periods at MORA. `r both_spans` The totals are in CCA distance, the rates in CCA distance per century.

# Associations with fire (Q3)

<!-- readme-only -->

**What and why.** Within the Holocene lake-periods, does a period with more climate change, or
more fire, end with a larger lag, and with better or worse pace and direction? Each response is
modelled on the park, the climate change rate and fire activity together. Consecutive
lake-periods of a lake can share an end century, so their errors are related, and an AR(1) term
on the order of the lake-periods within each lake carries that from the start. Ends that rest on
a single sample are noisier, so each row is weighted by the sampling variance of its two ends,
and the parks keep different residual spread. In the Anthropocene the same responses are
compared between burned and unburned plots within each park.

**How it is calculated.**

```{r step5-code}
code_snippet('R/pipeline/15_predictor_models.R', 'holocene-explanatory-model')
code_snippet('R/pipeline/15_predictor_models.R', 'anthropocene-explanatory-model')
```

**Result.**

<!-- /readme-only -->

```{r step5-results}
coefficients = read_output('community_predictor_models/model_coefficients.csv')
performance = read_output('community_predictor_models/model_performance.csv')
label = c(lag_rate = 'Lag rate', pace_effect = 'Pace effect', direction_effect = 'Direction effect',
  lag = 'Lag (not divided by time)', pace_effect_total = 'Pace effect (not divided by time)',
  direction_effect_total = 'Direction effect (not divided by time)')
coefficients |> left_join(performance |> select(metric = response, era, n, R2), by = c('metric', 'era')) |>
  transmute(Quantity = label[metric], Era = era, Term = term, Estimate = estimate, SE = std_error, df,
    t = estimate / std_error, `95% CI` = sprintf('%.3f to %.3f', conf_low, conf_high), p = p_value, n, `R²` = R2) |>
  show_table('step5_explanatory_models', caption = paste('**Table S21. Associations with fire: coefficients of the models.** Holocene:',
    'models of the lake-periods with park, climate change rate (or climate change, for the quantities not divided by time), and',
    'fire activity as fixed effects, a first-order autoregressive correlation within each lake, and weights for the number of',
    'samples at t1 and t2. Anthropocene: models of the plot pairs with park and fire (burned or unburned) as fixed effects (see',
    'Methods of the main text). Terms: siteNOCA, difference between NOCA and MORA; burnedBurned, difference between burned and',
    'unburned plot pairs. Estimates are in CCA distance (per century for the rates) for one unit of the term. SE, standard error.',
    'Two-sided t-tests on the residual degrees of freedom (df) of the model, with 95% confidence intervals (CI). n, number of',
    'lake-periods or plot pairs. R² is descriptive. The fit of the models is given in Table S22.'))
slope = function(m, t) coefficients |> filter(metric == m, era == 'Holocene', term == t)
f = function(x) sprintf('%+.2f (%.2f to %.2f)', x$estimate, x$conf_low, x$conf_high)
```

```{r step5-slope-words}
# The direction of each slope in words, from its interval, so that the text follows the fit.
say = function(m, t, what) {
  x = slope(m, t)
  if (x$conf_low > 0) sprintf('went with a larger %s (%s)', what, f(x))
  else if (x$conf_high < 0) sprintf('went with a smaller %s (%s)', what, f(x))
  else sprintf('did not go with the %s (%s)', what, f(x))
}
hol_slopes = coefficients |> filter(era == 'Holocene', term %in% c('climate_rate', 'climate_change', 'fire_activity'))
```

<!-- readme-only -->

In the Holocene, faster climate change `r say('lag_rate', 'climate_rate', 'lag rate')` and
`r say('pace_effect', 'climate_rate', 'pace effect')`. More frequent fire
`r say('lag_rate', 'fire_activity', 'lag rate')` and `r say('direction_effect', 'fire_activity', 'direction effect')`.
The slopes are in CCA distance per century for one more standardized unit of climate change per century,
or for one more event per century per core. The fire values of the two
parks barely overlap. The site term absorbs the difference between the parks, so the fire slope
comes from the narrow range within each park
(`r u = read_output('cca_tracking_lake_periods.csv'); paste(sprintf('%s %.2f to %.2f', c('MORA', 'NOCA'), tapply(u$fire_activity, u$site, min), tapply(u$fire_activity, u$site, max)), collapse = ', ')`
events per century per core).

The same models on the responses not divided by time use the climate change between the two ends in
place of its rate, and the slopes are in CCA distance per standardized unit of climate change or per
event per century per core. More climate change `r say('lag', 'climate_change', 'lag')`,
`r say('pace_effect_total', 'climate_change', 'pace effect')` and
`r say('direction_effect_total', 'climate_change', 'direction effect')`. More fire
`r say('lag', 'fire_activity', 'lag')`, `r say('pace_effect_total', 'fire_activity', 'pace effect')` and
`r say('direction_effect_total', 'fire_activity', 'direction effect')`. Of the
`r nrow(hol_slopes)` Holocene climate and fire slopes, `r n_away = sum(hol_slopes$conf_low > 0 | hol_slopes$conf_high < 0); n_away`
`r if (n_away == 1) 'has' else 'have'` an interval that excludes zero. They rest on `r nrow(u)` lake-periods and change markedly with the paleoclimate
correction (Appendix S4), so they are fragile. In the
Anthropocene, burned plots had a smaller total pace effect than unburned ones
(`r x = coefficients |> filter(metric == 'pace_effect_total', era == 'Anthropocene', term == 'burnedBurned'); f(x)`).
Fire activity stays a frequency in both forms, because a count of events would grow with the length
of the lake-period.

```{r fig-7-main}
perf6 = read_output('community_predictor_models/model_performance.csv')
R2 = function(r, e) sprintf('%.2f', perf6$R2[perf6$response == r & perf6$era == e])
```
